title: Japanese Bizen: Art that Rose from the Ashes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the ancient high-fired stoneware styles in Japan, none is as popular as Bizen pottery. Like many famous regional potteries, Bizen derives its name from the city it's produced: Imbe in Okayama, the Western Japan, and is a part of Japan's culture for its unique patterns and color schemes. It has an 800-year history and is considered one of the Six Ancient Kilns Perfections.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Bizen is believed as the jade out of the mud. The clay found in Imbe is sticky and fine, much organic matter that is unreceptive to glazing. For some potters this is an inadequate material, since it has weak characteristics such as high shrinkage and relatively low fire resistance. Most Bizen ware is not coated with a glaze because of this shrinkage, since any applied glaze would peel off during the firing process. However, the clay also has beneficial properties. The high strength causes it to retain the form, making the Bizen very tough.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A trailblazer in family’s history, Koichiro Isezaki carries on his generational ceramics practice of Bizen ware. He is the first son of Isezaki Jun, who is believed as the creator of Bizen ceramics and a living national treasure. Jun works closely with crafts from start to finish. As he makes the clay body from raw material, he the materials’ energy to use as the base of the work. Because of their extreme plasticity, Bizen wares are fired slowly and at most of times it takes in excess of 10 days. With careful consideration of material and composition, Jun creates a conversation between the interior and exterior of the finished piece and through technique and style, he brings life back into an old time-honored tradition.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An element of chance is inherent within the creation of Bizen ware ceramics, as they involve a glaze produced through natural burning materials inserted in the kiln during the firing process. In Bizen ware, the colors of the clay that surface depend on both iron and the type of firewood used. The less firewood, the more oxidizing the flame will be and, the vessels turn a bright reddish brown. Koichiro takes this a step further with his straying from tradition in order to come up with more creative and freer forms via multiple influences outside of his family. In his works, organized chaos and formed formlessness turn themselves on their head in order to produce something akin to his family’s work but with a more modern and textural twist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How is Bizen famous around Japan, even the whole world? Earth, water, wood and fire come together in harmony within the wildly dancing flames. The vessels, red hot and flashing, catch ash deposits from the firing process and create in a beautiful rhythm. Out of the kiln, each vessel reflects a natural gloss and bear traces of the flow of flames, rhythm of ash, and scent of the clay. ‘Breath of Clay' will feature works from Koichiro’s Yō series. The work contemplates the relationship between the interior and exterior, an idea conceived during his meditation of a tea ceremony. In anywhere, any world, it is a masterpiece without a doubt.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A cornerstone principle of Bizen Pottery is wabi-sabi - the concept, which originally comes from a combination of the words 'solitary' and ‘rustic’. Bizen Pottery celebrates the simplicity and asymmetry of nature in its individual and characterful works. It is pure and simple: combining the unrivaled skill of generations of potters with the beauty and abundance of nature from the region to create unique and singular pieces, completely unadulterated, with no added glazes or paints. It is the product of tremendous skill, shaped by nature.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is mysterious that there are no other potters that have exuded these characteristics at an unconscious level into all their works to the extent that Jun has. While the characteristics of Bizen ware are usually within any given pot, it is of course extraordinary for them to be found in a whole body of work. Anyone should be able to see, within Jun’s Bizen ware, the essential quality arising from long connection with the era. You will feel a charm in Bizen ware differing from those of the past. That new charm is surely a sublime radiance shining because the history of ceramics is like a backbone across the world of pottery, unchanging, despite one interruption, from ancient times to the modern world.
